**[1. Overview of Credit Facilities]{.underline}**
Ridgeline Environmental Services, Inc. (the \"Borrower\" or \"RES\"), a Colorado corporation with its principal offices in Denver, Colorado, is party to a Senior Secured Credit Agreement dated January 17, 2023 (the \"Credit Agreement\" or the \"Closing Date\") with High Plains National Bank, a nationally chartered banking institution headquartered in Denver, Colorado (the \"Lender\" or \"Administrative Agent\"). The Credit Agreement provides for a two-part senior secured credit facility consisting of a revolving credit facility and a term loan, each as described below.
**Senior Secured Revolving Credit Facility.** The Credit Agreement establishes a revolving credit facility in the aggregate commitment amount of \$25,000,000. Borrowings under the revolving facility are subject to a borrowing base consisting of eligible accounts receivable (at an 85% advance rate) and eligible inventory (at a 50% advance rate), each as defined in the Credit Agreement and certified monthly by the Borrower. As of September 30, 2024, the outstanding balance under the revolving facility was \$12,400,000, leaving available capacity of \$12,600,000. The revolving facility matures on January 17, 2028, which is the fifth anniversary of the Closing Date. The revolving facility also provides for the issuance of letters of credit, which reduce available borrowing capacity on a dollar-for-dollar basis.
**Senior Secured Term Loan.** The Credit Agreement also provides for a term loan in the original principal amount of \$26,300,000, funded in full on the Closing Date. The term loan is structured as interest-only for the first twenty-four months following the Closing Date (through January 17, 2025), after which quarterly principal amortization payments of \$657,500 commence (representing 2.5% of the original principal amount per quarter). The remaining outstanding balance is due in full at maturity on January 17, 2028. As of September 30, 2024, the outstanding principal balance of the term loan was \$26,300,000, as no amortization payments had yet become due during the interest-only period.
**Aggregate Outstanding Debt.** As of September 30, 2024, total funded debt under the Credit Agreement was \$38,700,000, consisting of \$12,400,000 under the revolving facility and \$26,300,000 under the term loan.
**Guarantors.** All obligations under the Credit Agreement are guaranteed by all existing and future domestic subsidiaries of the Borrower. As of the date of this summary, the sole subsidiary guarantor is Pinnacle Waste Solutions, LLC, a wholly-owned Utah limited liability company that was acquired by the Borrower on March 15, 2022. Pinnacle was joined as a Guarantor pursuant to a Joinder Agreement dated March 15, 2022, which was subsequently ratified under the Credit Agreement and formalized by the First Amendment dated March 28, 2023. The guarantee is full, unconditional, and irrevocable, and is secured by substantially all assets of the Guarantor, including the equity interests held by the Borrower in Pinnacle.
**[2. Interest Rates and Fees]{.underline}**
**Revolving Facility Interest Rate.** Borrowings under the revolving facility bear interest at a rate equal to the Secured Overnight Financing Rate (\"SOFR\") plus an applicable margin determined by reference to the Borrower\'s total leverage ratio as of the most recent compliance certificate delivery date. The applicable margin grid is as follows:
 **Total Leverage Ratio** **Applicable Margin**
 -- --
 ≤ 1.50x SOFR + 2.25%
 \> 1.50x and ≤ 2.50x SOFR + 2.50%
 \> 2.50x and ≤ 3.00x SOFR + 2.75%
 \> 3.00x SOFR + 3.00%
Based on the most recent compliance certificate delivered for the fiscal quarter ending September 30, 2024, the Borrower\'s total leverage ratio was 2.10x (calculated using Consolidated EBITDA as defined by the Credit Agreement --- see Section 4 below), resulting in a current applicable margin of SOFR + 2.50%.
**Term Loan Interest Rate.** The term loan bears interest at a fixed spread of SOFR + 3.25%, regardless of the Borrower\'s leverage ratio. There is no pricing grid applicable to the term loan.
**Unused Line Fee.** The Borrower pays an unused line fee equal to 0.375% per annum on the daily average unused portion of the revolving commitment, payable quarterly in arrears.
**Letter of Credit Fee.** Outstanding letters of credit are subject to a fee of 2.50% per annum on the face amount, plus a \$500 issuance fee per letter of credit.
**Default Rate.** During the continuance of any Event of Default, all outstanding obligations bear interest at an additional 2.00% per annum above the otherwise applicable rate.

**[4. Definition of EBITDA (Bank Definition)]{.underline}**
The definition of Consolidated EBITDA under the Credit Agreement is critical for purposes of evaluating covenant compliance and should be carefully distinguished from the management-prepared adjusted EBITDA figures presented elsewhere in the data room.
**\"Consolidated EBITDA\"** is defined in Section 1.01 of the Credit Agreement as consolidated net income of the Borrower and its subsidiaries, determined in accordance with GAAP, plus, to the extent deducted in calculating consolidated net income: (a) interest expense, (b) income tax expense, (c) depreciation and amortization expense, (d) non-cash stock-based compensation expense, and (e) non-recurring, extraordinary losses or charges in an aggregate amount not to exceed \$500,000 in any fiscal year.
**Excluded Add-Backs.** The Credit Agreement expressly provides that the following items shall not be added back or otherwise included in the calculation of Consolidated EBITDA: (i) management fees, consulting fees, or transaction-related fees paid to equity holders; (ii) one-time cost savings, synergies, or restructuring adjustments; (iii) add-backs for discontinued operations or service line wind-downs; (iv) normalization adjustments to owner or officer compensation; and (v) any adjustments not in accordance with GAAP.
**Significance for Covenant Calculations.** The bank\'s Consolidated EBITDA definition produces a materially different figure than management\'s adjusted EBITDA. For the trailing twelve-month period ending September 30, 2024, Consolidated EBITDA per the bank definition was approximately \$18.4 million --- essentially reported EBITDA with minimal qualifying add-backs. Management\'s adjusted EBITDA of \$22.8 million (as presented in the Confidential Information Memorandum) or \$23.8 million (per the detailed adjustment schedule) includes approximately \$5.4 million in adjustments that do not qualify under the Credit Agreement definition. Specifically, the following management adjustments are not permitted add-backs under the bank definition:
> • Litigation settlement costs: \$1,200,000
>
> • Owner compensation normalization: \$950,000
>
> • ERP implementation costs: \$650,000
>
> • Pinnacle acquisition-related expenses: \$800,000
>
> • Asbestos abatement service line wind-down costs: \$1,800,000
Of these amounts, only up to \$500,000 could potentially qualify as non-recurring extraordinary charges under clause (e) of the Consolidated EBITDA definition.
**Resulting Leverage Calculation.** Total funded debt of \$38,700,000 divided by Consolidated EBITDA of approximately \$18,400,000 yields a total leverage ratio of approximately 2.10x under the bank definition, which is within the 3.50x maximum covenant level. If management\'s adjusted EBITDA of \$22.8 million or \$23.8 million were used instead, leverage would calculate to approximately 1.70x or 1.62x, respectively --- but those figures are not relevant for covenant compliance under the Credit Agreement.
**[5. Financial Covenants]{.underline}**
The Credit Agreement requires the Borrower to maintain compliance with the following financial covenants, tested as of the last day of each fiscal quarter based on trailing four-quarter results:
**Maximum Total Leverage Ratio.** Total funded debt divided by Consolidated EBITDA (bank definition, trailing four quarters) shall not exceed 3.50x. As of September 30, 2024, the Borrower\'s total leverage ratio was approximately 2.10x (\$38,700,000 / \$18,400,000), providing covenant headroom of approximately 1.40x.
**Minimum Fixed Charge Coverage Ratio.** The ratio of (Consolidated EBITDA minus unfinanced capital expenditures minus cash taxes paid minus distributions) to (scheduled principal payments plus cash interest payments) shall not be less than 1.25x. The Borrower\'s most recent compliance certificate for the period ending September 30, 2024 reports a fixed charge coverage ratio of 1.68x.
**Minimum Liquidity.** The Borrower must maintain minimum availability under the revolving facility of not less than \$5,000,000 at all times. As of September 30, 2024, availability was \$12,600,000 (\$25,000,000 commitment less \$12,400,000 outstanding), satisfying this requirement.
**Testing and Certification.** Financial covenant compliance is tested quarterly, with compliance certificates signed by the Chief Financial Officer due within 45 days of each fiscal quarter end. **[8. Change of Control Provision]{.underline}**
**Definition of \"Change of Control.\"** A \"Change of Control\" is defined in Section 1.01 of the Credit Agreement as any of the following events:
> \(a\) Derek Calloway and Jason Calloway, together with the Calloway Family Trust, cease to own, directly or indirectly, at least 51% of the outstanding equity interests of the Borrower;
>
> \(b\) Derek Calloway ceases to serve as Chief Executive Officer of the Borrower (unless a successor is approved in writing by the Lender within 90 days of such cessation);
>
> \(c\) any \"person\" or \"group\" (within the meaning of Section 13(d) or 14(d) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934) acquires, directly or indirectly, beneficial ownership of 50% or more of the outstanding equity interests of the Borrower; or
>
> \(d\) the Borrower merges with or into, or consolidates with, any other entity unless the Borrower is the surviving entity and the conditions of clause (a) above continue to be satisfied immediately following such merger or consolidation.
**Mandatory Prepayment upon Change of Control.** Section 2.11(c) of the Credit Agreement provides that upon the occurrence of a Change of Control, the Borrower shall immediately notify the Lender and shall, within **five (5) business days** following such Change of Control, prepay in full all outstanding Obligations under the Credit Agreement. \"Obligations\" includes all outstanding principal, accrued and unpaid interest, fees, and any applicable prepayment premium (as described in Section 9 below). As of September 30, 2024, total outstanding Obligations under the Credit Agreement include \$12,400,000 under the revolving facility and \$26,300,000 under the term loan, for an aggregate funded principal balance of **\$38,700,000**, plus accrued and unpaid interest and applicable fees.
**Revolver Commitment Termination.** Upon the occurrence of a Change of Control, the revolving commitment shall be permanently reduced to zero and all outstanding letters of credit must be cash collateralized at 105% of face amount.
**Application to Proposed Transaction.** The Change of Control definition would be triggered by the proposed acquisition of 100% of the outstanding equity of RES by Sycamore Capital Partners, LP. The proposed transaction contemplates the acquisition of all outstanding equity interests from Derek Calloway (32.5%), Jason Calloway (32.5%), and the Calloway Family Trust (35%), such that Sycamore would acquire 100% of the equity interests in the Borrower. This would trigger clause (c) of the Change of Control definition (acquisition of 50% or more by a person or group) and clause (a) (the Calloway family members ceasing to hold at least 51%).
**No Consent or Waiver Mechanism.** The Credit Agreement does not provide a mechanism to waive or obtain consent to a Change of Control in lieu of prepayment. The only alternatives available to the Borrower would be to negotiate a payoff letter or arrange refinancing with High Plains National Bank (or a replacement lender) in advance of closing the proposed transaction.

**[Section 1: Overview]{.underline}**
Ridgeline Environmental Services, Inc. (\"RES\" or the \"Company\") is headquartered at 8750 Industrial Parkway, Grand Junction, CO 81505. The Company was founded in 2009 and currently employs approximately 485 full-time equivalent employees (\"FTEs\") across 11 facilities in Colorado, Utah, Wyoming, Montana, and Idaho. The workforce supports the Company\'s four primary service lines: environmental remediation (approximately 45% of revenue), hazardous waste transportation and disposal (approximately 25%), emergency spill response (approximately 18%), and industrial cleaning (approximately 12%). The Company does not employ any part-time or seasonal workers on a regular basis, though temporary staffing is utilized for surge demand in emergency spill response. Following the acquisition of Pinnacle Waste Solutions, LLC in March 2022, approximately 38 Pinnacle employees were integrated into the RES workforce. The information presented in this summary reflects the Company\'s current workforce as of the date hereof, and all financial figures are based on the trailing twelve-month period ending September 30, 2024, unless otherwise indicated.

**[Section 4: Benefits Programs]{.underline}**
**4.1 Health, Dental, and Vision Insurance**
RES offers a group health insurance program to all full-time employees, with coverage effective on the first day of the month following 60 days of continuous employment. The plans are administered through a fully-insured arrangement with Anthem Blue Cross Blue Shield. Coverage is available in four tiers: Employee Only, Employee + Spouse, Employee + Children, and Family. The Company contributes approximately 70% of the Employee Only premium and approximately 50% of dependent premiums for all coverage tiers. The current annual employer cost for group health insurance is approximately \$3.1 million. Dental and vision coverage are offered as voluntary, employee-paid benefits through Delta Dental and VSP Vision Care, respectively. As of September 30, 2024, approximately 82% of eligible employees participate in the health plan, dental participation is approximately 61%, and vision participation is approximately 44%.
**4.2 401(k) Retirement Plan**
The Company sponsors a safe harbor 401(k) plan (the \"Plan\") for all employees who have completed 90 days of service and have attained age 21. The Plan provides for a safe harbor employer matching contribution equal to 100% of the first 3% of eligible compensation deferred by the participant, plus 50% of the next 2% of eligible compensation deferred, resulting in a maximum employer matching contribution of 4% of eligible compensation. Employee contributions are immediately 100% vested, and employer matching contributions are also 100% vested under the safe harbor provisions. Due to operational cash flow management requirements, the employer matching contribution was temporarily suspended from January 1, 2023 through June 30, 2023. Matching contributions resumed at the full safe harbor level effective July 1, 2023.
The Plan is administered by the Company\'s Human Resources department, with Patricia Engel, CFO, serving as the named Plan administrator. Plan assets are held with Fidelity Investments, which serves as third-party recordkeeper and custodian. As of September 30, 2024, total Plan assets were approximately \$14.8 million. Approximately 71% of eligible employees actively contribute to the Plan. The Company estimates its annual employer matching cost at approximately \$1.1 million, based on FY2024 actual contributions for the period July 2023 through September 2024, annualized.
**4.3 Paid Time Off (PTO)**
RES provides a consolidated Paid Time Off program that combines vacation, sick, and personal days into a single PTO bank. PTO accrues on a per-pay-period basis according to the following schedule based on years of continuous service:
 **Years of Service** **Annual PTO Entitlement**
 -- --
 0--2 years 15 days
 3--5 years 20 days
 6--10 years 25 days
 10+ years 30 days
The maximum accrual cap is 1.5 times the employee\'s annual PTO entitlement. Unused PTO is paid out upon termination in Colorado and Utah, consistent with applicable state law requirements. In Wyoming, Montana, and Idaho, unused PTO is forfeited upon termination per company policy, which the Company believes is consistent with applicable state law. As of September 30, 2024, the Company\'s aggregate accrued PTO liability was approximately \$1.4 million.
**4.4 Other Benefits**
The Company provides the following additional benefits to eligible employees:
> • **Life Insurance:** Employer-paid basic life insurance coverage of \$50,000 per employee; supplemental voluntary life insurance is available at group rates for employees and their dependents.
>
> • **Short-Term Disability:** Employer-paid coverage providing 60% of base salary with a 13-week maximum benefit period.
>
> • **Long-Term Disability:** Voluntary, employee-paid coverage providing 60% of base salary following the short-term disability benefit period.
>
> • **Employee Assistance Program (EAP):** Available to all employees and their dependents at no cost, providing confidential counseling, crisis support, and referral services.
>
> • **Tuition Reimbursement:** Up to \$5,000 per year for job-related education, subject to management approval and satisfactory completion of coursework.
>
> • **Safety Bonus Program:** Quarterly safety incentive bonuses for field personnel, averaging \$500 to \$1,500 per quarter per eligible employee, based on incident-free performance metrics and compliance with the Company\'s health, safety, and environmental protocols.
**[Section 5: Executive Compensation Overview]{.underline}**
Detailed executive employment agreements and compensation arrangements are summarized separately in the data room (see Employment Agreements Summary). For purposes of this benefits summary, all five named executives --- Chief Executive Officer Derek Calloway, Chief Operating Officer Jason Calloway, Chief Financial Officer Patricia Engel, Vice President of Operations Kurt Dillon, and Vice President of Business Development Sandra Oakes --- participate in the same group health insurance and 401(k) retirement plans available to all other Company employees under the terms described in Section 4 above. Executive bonuses are discretionary and are typically targeted at 30% to 50% of base salary, based on Company performance and individual contributions. The Company does not currently maintain a nonqualified deferred compensation plan, equity incentive plan, stock option plan, or supplemental executive retirement plan.
**[Section 6: Workers\' Compensation and Safety]{.underline}**
Workers\' compensation insurance is maintained through Frontier Specialty Insurance Group at statutory limits for all five operating states (Colorado, Utah, Wyoming, Montana, and Idaho). The Company\'s current Experience Modification Rate (EMR) is 0.94, which is below the industry baseline of 1.0, reflecting a favorable claims history over the applicable experience period. The Company employs 17 Health, Safety & Environmental (HSE) professionals across its facilities and maintains a comprehensive OSHA-compliant safety program, including regular training, job hazard analyses, and incident investigation protocols. The Company\'s OSHA Total Recordable Incident Rate (TRIR) for FY2024 was 2.8, compared to the NAICS 562910 (Remediation Services) industry average of approximately 3.4. There have been no OSHA citations issued against the Company in the past three years. One personal injury claim, *Ramirez v. Ridgeline Environmental Services, Inc.*, Case No. 2:24-cv-00187 (D. Wyo.), was filed August 12, 2024 by a former employee. This matter is addressed in detail in the Litigation and Regulatory Summary included separately in the data room.
**[Section 7: Labor Relations]{.underline}**
The Company does not currently have any collective bargaining agreement in effect. The workforce is non-unionized.¹ The Company maintains an open-door policy and conducts annual employee satisfaction surveys to monitor workforce morale and identify areas for improvement. The most recent employee satisfaction survey, conducted in June 2024, showed an overall satisfaction rating of 72%, which is consistent with results from prior years. Management believes that its compensation, benefits, and safety programs contribute to a generally positive working environment across the Company\'s operations.
**[Section 8: Recent HR Developments]{.underline}**
The following notable workforce developments occurred during FY2024:
> • **Pinnacle Integration Complete.** The Company completed the integration of former Pinnacle Waste Solutions, LLC employees during FY2023. All 38 former Pinnacle employees have been fully onboarded onto RES systems, benefits platforms, and payroll, and are reflected in the headcount figures presented in Section 2 above.
>
> • **HRIS System Implementation.** The Company implemented a new Human Resources Information System (as a module of the broader ERP implementation) in Q1 FY2024, consolidating employee records, benefits administration, and time-tracking across all 11 facilities.
>
> • **Asbestos Abatement Wind-Down.** The Company wound down its asbestos abatement service line effective September 30, 2023. Approximately 14 employees previously assigned to this service line were reassigned to other operational divisions; 8 employees were separated with standard severance packages in accordance with Company policy.
>
> • **New VP Business Development.** The Company hired Sandra Oakes as Vice President of Business Development in February 2024, a newly created position established to support the Company\'s growth initiatives and strategic planning efforts.
>
> • **FY2025 Outlook.** No material workforce reductions or restructurings are planned for FY2025. The Company anticipates modest headcount growth in its field operations and emergency response functions consistent with projected revenue increases.

**[Section 3: Detailed Narrative --- Derek Calloway, Chief Executive Officer]{.underline}**
Derek Calloway co-founded Ridgeline Environmental Services in 2009 and has served as Chief Executive Officer since the Company\'s inception. His employment agreement was originally executed in 2009 and was subsequently amended and restated effective January 1, 2018, to reflect updated compensation terms and expanded restrictive covenants.
**Compensation.** Mr. Calloway\'s current base salary is \$875,000 per annum, subject to annual review and adjustment by the Board of Directors. The base salary has been at the \$875,000 level since FY2022. His annual performance bonus target is 50% of base salary (\$437,500), based on the Company\'s achievement of revenue growth, EBITDA targets, and safety metrics as established by the Board at the beginning of each fiscal year. The bonus is discretionary and, in exceptional performance years, may exceed the target up to a maximum of 100% of base salary (\$875,000).
**Change-of-Control Provision.** Upon a Change of Control (as defined above), Mr. Calloway is entitled to a lump-sum severance payment equal to 18 months of base salary plus the target annual bonus, totaling \$875,000 × 1.5 = \$1,312,500. Payment is due within 30 days of the closing of the Change of Control transaction. Importantly, the severance is payable regardless of whether Mr. Calloway\'s employment is terminated, modified, or continues following the closing. This is a \"single trigger\" provision --- no employment-related event beyond the Change of Control itself is required to trigger the payment obligation.
**Restrictive Covenants.** For a period of 2 years following termination of employment for any reason, Mr. Calloway shall not directly or indirectly engage in any business competitive with the Company\'s environmental remediation, hazardous waste transportation and disposal, emergency spill response, or industrial cleaning services within the states of Colorado, Utah, Wyoming, Montana, and Idaho. The agreement also contains a 2-year non-solicitation covenant covering employees, customers, and vendors of the Company.
**Termination Without Cause.** In the event of termination without Cause (outside the change-of-control context), Mr. Calloway is entitled to 12 months\' base salary severance (\$875,000), plus a prorated bonus for the year of termination. Termination for Cause results in no severance; Cause is defined to include conviction of a felony, material breach of the agreement, and willful misconduct.
**Benefits and Equity.** Mr. Calloway is entitled to participation in all executive benefit plans, including health, dental, vision, and the Company\'s 401(k) retirement plan. **[1. Introduction and Purpose]{.underline}**
Elkhorn Environmental Consultants, Inc. (\"Elkhorn\") was retained by Ridgeline Environmental Services, Inc. (\"RES\" or the \"Client\") to conduct a Phase II Environmental Site Assessment (\"Phase II ESA\") at the property located at 8750 Industrial Parkway, Grand Junction, Mesa County, Colorado 81505 (the \"Site\" or \"Property\"). This Executive Summary presents the principal findings, conclusions, and recommendations of the Phase II ESA. The full Phase II ESA report, comprising approximately 180 pages with supporting appendices, is available upon request from RES and should be consulted for complete analytical data, interpretive analysis, and technical detail.
The assessment was conducted in accordance with ASTM E1903-11, *Standard Practice for Environmental Site Assessments: Phase II Environmental Site Assessment Process*, and applicable guidance documents published by the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment (\"CDPHE\"). All field investigation activities, laboratory analyses, and data interpretation were performed consistent with these standards and with generally accepted environmental consulting practices.
The purpose of this Phase II ESA was to evaluate recognized environmental conditions (\"RECs\") identified during a prior Phase I Environmental Site Assessment completed by Elkhorn (Project No. EEC-2018-0891, dated November 2018). The Phase I ESA identified the following RECs warranting subsurface investigation:
> \(i\) Historical use of the eastern portion of the Site for petroleum product storage and distribution operations from approximately 1972 through 2005;
>
> \(ii\) Reported releases of chlorinated solvents, including tetrachloroethylene (\"PCE\") and trichloroethylene (\"TCE\"), associated with former industrial parts cleaning and degreasing operations conducted by a prior occupant from approximately 1985 through 2003; and
>
> \(iii\) The presence of two former underground storage tanks (\"USTs\") removed in 2006 by a previous property owner, with incomplete closure documentation and residual contamination identified in confirmation sampling.
RES acquired the Property in 2009 and has operated it continuously since that date as its corporate headquarters and primary operations facility. RES\'s current operations at the Site involve the storage, handling, consolidation, and transportation of hazardous wastes under Colorado RCRA Part B Permit No. COD-098-2761, which was renewed in 2021 and is valid through December 31, 2026. RES did not conduct or cause the historical industrial operations that are the source of the contamination investigated in this assessment. RES was founded in 2009 by Derek Calloway and Jason Calloway, and the Grand Junction facility has served as the company\'s base of operations since its inception.
**[2. Site Description and History]{.underline}**
**2.1 Site Description**
The Property comprises approximately 12.4 acres of developed industrial land situated along the south side of Industrial Parkway in Grand Junction, Colorado. The Site is improved with the following principal structures and features:
> \(a\) A 42,000-square-foot main office and warehouse building, constructed circa 1975 and renovated in 2010, which serves as the primary administrative offices and indoor storage area for RES;
>
> \(b\) A 28,000-square-foot vehicle maintenance and equipment storage building, constructed circa 1982, located in the eastern portion of the Site, used by RES for fleet maintenance and equipment staging;
>
> \(c\) A 15,000-square-foot hazardous waste staging and consolidation building, constructed circa 1990 and modified by RES in 2012 to meet current RCRA requirements, used for temporary storage and consolidation of hazardous wastes prior to off-site shipment;
>
> \(d\) Paved truck yards and parking areas encompassing approximately 4.5 acres, used for vehicle circulation, equipment staging, and employee parking; and
>
> \(e\) Ancillary structures including a stormwater detention pond, perimeter fencing, a truck scale house, and utility buildings.
The Property is bounded to the north by Industrial Parkway, to the east by undeveloped land administered by the Bureau of Land Management (\"BLM\"), to the south by an active railroad right-of-way (Union Pacific Railroad), and to the west by an active industrial facility engaged in metal fabrication operations.
**2.2 Topography and Hydrogeology**
The Site is situated on a relatively flat alluvial terrace at an elevation of approximately 4,590 feet above mean sea level. The terrain slopes gently to the northwest at a gradient of approximately 0.5 percent. Shallow groundwater is encountered at depths of approximately 18 to 25 feet below ground surface (\"bgs\") within unconsolidated alluvial deposits consisting of interbedded sands, gravels, silts, and clays. Regional groundwater flow is generally to the northwest toward the Colorado River, which is located approximately 1.2 miles north-northwest of the Site. The alluvial aquifer is unconfined and exhibits seasonal water table fluctuations of approximately 3 feet based on available regional data from the Colorado Division of Water Resources.
**2.3 Site History Summary**
Based on information compiled during the Phase I ESA, the operational history of the Site is summarized as follows:
**1972--2005:** The Site was originally developed and operated as a petroleum product storage and distribution facility by a succession of owners, including Western Slope Petroleum, Inc. (1972--1988) and Grand Valley Fuels, LLC (1988--2005). Operations included bulk storage and distribution of gasoline, diesel fuel, and heating oil.
**1985--2003:** Portions of the eastern building complex were used by Grand Valley Fuels, LLC and its subtenants for industrial parts cleaning and degreasing operations. These operations involved the use of chlorinated solvents, primarily PCE and TCE, in open-top vapor degreasers and parts washing systems.
**2006:** Two 10,000-gallon USTs --- one diesel and one gasoline --- were removed by the then-owner. A closure report was submitted to the Colorado Division of Oil and Public Safety; however, analytical data from confirmation soil samples collected during the tank removal indicated residual contamination at concentrations exceeding applicable screening levels. A No Further Action (\"NFA\") letter was not issued by the Division, and the closure file remains open.
**2007--2009:** The Site was vacant and unoccupied following the cessation of petroleum distribution operations.
**2009--Present:** RES acquired the Property and commenced operations. RES has operated the facility continuously since 2009 for hazardous waste management services. RES\'s operations have not contributed to the pre-existing contamination at the Site.
**[3. Scope of Investigation]{.underline}**
**3.1 Field Activities**
Field investigation activities were conducted between April 22 and May 10, 2019 under the direct supervision of Dr. Thomas Hargrove, P.G. The scope of investigation included the following:
**Soil Borings:** A total of 24 soil borings (designated SB-01 through SB-24) were advanced to depths ranging from 5 to 35 feet bgs using a truck-mounted hollow-stem auger drill rig. Borings were positioned to delineate the lateral and vertical extent of contamination in the two identified source areas (the former UST area in the western portion of the Site and the former degreasing operations area in the eastern portion of the Site), as well as in areas of potential contaminant migration. Continuous split-spoon soil samples were collected at 2-foot intervals and were field-screened using a photoionization detector (\"PID\"). A total of 72 discrete soil samples were submitted for laboratory analysis.
**Groundwater Monitoring Wells:** Six temporary groundwater monitoring wells (designated MW-01 through MW-06) were installed at strategic locations across the Site, screened across the water table in the alluvial aquifer. Wells were constructed of 2-inch diameter Schedule 40 PVC casing with 10-foot factory-slotted screens (0.010-inch slot size). Wells were developed a minimum of 24 hours prior to sampling. A total of 12 groundwater samples were collected (two sampling rounds, one in April and one in May 2019) using low-flow purging techniques in accordance with CDPHE guidance.
**Soil Gas Survey:** Fifteen soil gas implants (designated SG-01 through SG-15) were installed at depths of approximately 5 feet bgs across the eastern and central portions of the Site. Soil gas samples were collected after a minimum 48-hour equilibration period using summa canisters with calibrated flow controllers.
**Geophysical Survey:** A ground-penetrating radar (\"GPR\") survey was conducted over the former UST area and adjacent regions to evaluate the presence of potential subsurface anomalies, including remnant piping, backfill materials, or previously unidentified buried structures.
**3.2 Laboratory Analysis**
All samples were submitted under chain-of-custody protocols to Granite Peak Analytical Laboratories, Inc. (\"Granite Peak\"), a CDPHE-certified laboratory (Certificate No. CO-LAB-2017-0443, Denver, Colorado). Analytical parameters and methods were as follows:
**Soil Samples:** BTEX compounds (benzene, toluene, ethylbenzene, and xylenes); total petroleum hydrocarbons as diesel-range organics (\"TPH-DRO\") and gasoline-range organics (\"TPH-GRO\") by EPA Method 8015; volatile organic compounds (\"VOCs\") by EPA Method 8260; and semi-volatile organic compounds (\"SVOCs\") by EPA Method 8270.
**Groundwater Samples:** Full VOC suite by EPA Method 8260; TPH by EPA Method 8015; dissolved metals by EPA Methods 6010 and 7470.
**Soil Gas Samples:** VOCs by EPA Method TO-15.
**3.3 Applicable Screening Criteria**
Analytical results were compared against the following applicable screening criteria: (i) CDPHE Soil Cleanup Levels for residential and commercial/industrial land use; (ii) Colorado Basic Standards for Groundwater (Regulation No. 41, 5 CCR 1002-41); and (iii) EPA Regional Screening Levels (\"RSLs\") for soil gas in a commercial/industrial setting.
**[4. Findings --- Soil Contamination]{.underline}**
**4.1 Area 1 --- Former UST Area (Western Site)**
Soil sampling in the former UST area confirmed the presence of petroleum hydrocarbon contamination at concentrations exceeding applicable CDPHE commercial/industrial soil cleanup levels. Key results include:
> • TPH-diesel was detected at concentrations up to 4,200 mg/kg at boring SB-03 (8--10 ft bgs), exceeding the CDPHE commercial/industrial soil cleanup level of 2,800 mg/kg. Elevated TPH-diesel was also detected in borings SB-02, SB-04, and SB-06 at concentrations ranging from 1,400 to 3,100 mg/kg.
>
> • TPH-gasoline was detected at concentrations up to 890 mg/kg at boring SB-05 (6--8 ft bgs), exceeding the CDPHE commercial/industrial soil cleanup level of 500 mg/kg. TPH-gasoline was also detected above screening levels in borings SB-03 and SB-04.
>
> • BTEX compounds were detected in multiple borings within the former UST area. Benzene was detected at a maximum concentration of 2.4 mg/kg at boring SB-04 (10--12 ft bgs), exceeding the CDPHE commercial/industrial soil cleanup level of 1.2 mg/kg.
The lateral extent of petroleum contamination in Area 1 is estimated at approximately 8,500 square feet, extending from the former UST excavation area eastward toward the main office and warehouse building. Vertical extent ranges from near the ground surface to approximately 16 feet bgs, which in most locations remains above the water table. The GPR survey confirmed the location of the former UST excavation and identified remnant product piping extending approximately 40 feet east of the former tank cavity.
**4.2 Area 2 --- Former Degreasing Operations Area (Eastern Site)**
Soil sampling in the area of former degreasing operations confirmed the presence of chlorinated solvent contamination at concentrations significantly exceeding applicable CDPHE commercial/industrial soil cleanup levels. Key results include:
> • PCE was detected at concentrations up to 18 mg/kg at boring SB-14 (12--14 ft bgs), exceeding the CDPHE commercial/industrial soil cleanup level of 3.4 mg/kg. PCE was also detected above screening levels in borings SB-12, SB-13, SB-15, SB-16, and SB-17.
>
> • TCE was detected at concentrations up to 6.8 mg/kg at boring SB-15 (14--16 ft bgs), exceeding the CDPHE commercial/industrial soil cleanup level of 2.3 mg/kg.
>
> • Cis-1,2-dichloroethylene (\"cis-1,2-DCE\"), a reductive dechlorination daughter product of TCE, was detected at concentrations up to 3.1 mg/kg at boring SB-14 (16--18 ft bgs). The presence of cis-1,2-DCE indicates that active biodegradation of chlorinated solvents is occurring in the subsurface but also confirms an ongoing contaminant source.
Chlorinated solvent contamination extends laterally over an area of approximately 12,000 square feet in the eastern portion of the Site and vertically from approximately 6 feet bgs to the water table (encountered at approximately 22 feet bgs in this area). The contamination geometry is consistent with a diffuse, vertically migrating plume rather than a discrete point source.
**4.3 Contamination Release Characterization**
The contamination at both Area 1 and Area 2 is characterized as resulting from **gradual releases** over extended periods of time --- spanning multiple decades --- rather than sudden or accidental discharges. The petroleum hydrocarbon contamination in Area 1 is consistent with chronic, low-volume releases from aging UST systems and associated product distribution piping over the approximately 33-year period of petroleum operations (1972--2005). The contamination pattern --- including diffuse lateral distribution, the absence of a discrete point-source feature, and the depth-distributed contaminant profile --- is indicative of prolonged, incremental releases rather than a single catastrophic failure event.
Similarly, the chlorinated solvent contamination in Area 2 exhibits characteristics consistent with prolonged, incremental releases from degreasing operations and/or improper storage and disposal practices over an approximately 18-year period (1985--2003). The presence of reductive dechlorination byproducts (cis-1,2-DCE), the diffuse plume geometry, and the broad vertical distribution of contaminants all support a characterization of gradual, long-term releases rather than a sudden or accidental discharge.
**4.4 Contaminant Migration Potential**
Given the proximity of both contamination areas to the water table, there is a potential for continued downward migration of contaminants from soil into groundwater. This risk is particularly significant for the chlorinated solvents in Area 2, as PCE and TCE are denser-than-water non-aqueous phase liquids (\"DNAPLs\") that, once reaching the water table, tend to migrate vertically through the aquifer rather than remaining at the water table surface. Seasonal fluctuations in the water table (observed to vary approximately 3 feet based on regional data) may result in periodic smearing of contaminants across the capillary fringe zone, expanding the zone of impact. Elkhorn recommends periodic monitoring to assess whether the contamination plume has stabilized or is actively migrating, and to evaluate whether contaminant concentrations in groundwater are increasing, stable, or decreasing over time.
**[5. Findings --- Groundwater Contamination]{.underline}**
**5.1 Monitoring Well Results**
Groundwater sampling from the six temporary monitoring wells (two rounds: April and May 2019) yielded the following significant results:
**MW-02** (located approximately 50 f

eet downgradient of the former UST area): Benzene was detected at a concentration of 12 µg/L, exceeding the Colorado Basic Standard for Groundwater of 5 µg/L. TPH-diesel was detected at 340 µg/L. Toluene, ethylbenzene, and xylenes were detected but at concentrations below applicable standards.
**MW-04** (located approximately 40 feet downgradient of the former degreasing operations area): PCE was detected at a concentration of 22 µg/L, exceeding the Colorado Basic Standard of 5 µg/L. TCE was detected at 8.7 µg/L, also exceeding the Colorado Basic Standard of 5 µg/L. Cis-1,2-DCE was detected at 15 µg/L, which is below the applicable Colorado Basic Standard of 70 µg/L.
**MW-01, MW-03, MW-05, MW-06:** No analytes were detected at concentrations exceeding applicable Colorado Basic Standards for Groundwater. Background conditions appear unaffected in these locations.
**5.2 Interpretation.** The groundwater analytical results confirm that contamination from the two historical source areas has impacted the shallow alluvial aquifer. The contamination detected in groundwater is consistent with the soil findings and represents impact from the same historical gradual releases documented in the soil data. Based on the current monitoring well network, the groundwater contamination plume appears to be localized in the immediate vicinity of the two source areas and does not appear to have migrated off-site. However, Elkhorn notes that the monitoring well coverage is limited to the Property boundaries and does not include any off-site sentinel wells. Accordingly, this conclusion regarding plume containment should be considered preliminary.
**5.3 Recommendation.** Elkhorn recommends the installation of at least two off-site downgradient monitoring wells --- one northwest of the former UST area and one northwest of the former degreasing area --- to confirm that the groundwater contamination plume has not migrated beyond the Property boundary toward the Colorado River drainage system. If off-site migration is confirmed, additional regulatory notification requirements under Colorado Regulation No. 41 may be triggered, which could materially increase the scope, complexity, and cost of required remediation.
**[6. Findings --- Soil Gas]{.underline}**
**6.1 Soil Gas Analytical Results**
Soil gas sampling detected elevated concentrations of chlorinated solvent vapors at two locations in the eastern portion of the Site:
**SG-09** (adjacent to the eastern wall of the vehicle maintenance building): PCE at 450 µg/m³, exceeding the EPA Regional Screening Level for commercial/industrial land use of 240 µg/m³. TCE at 120 µg/m³, exceeding the EPA RSL of 21 µg/m³.
**SG-10** (approximately 25 feet south of SG-09): PCE at 310 µg/m³, exceeding the EPA RSL. TCE at 87 µg/m³, exceeding the EPA RSL.
**SG-07, SG-08, SG-11 through SG-15:** All target analytes were detected at concentrations below applicable EPA Regional Screening Levels.
Soil gas implants SG-01 through SG-06, located in the western and central portions of the Site, did not detect chlorinated solvent vapors above reporting limits.
**6.2 Vapor Intrusion Risk**
The soil gas results at SG-09 and SG-10 indicate a potential vapor intrusion pathway into the 28,000-square-foot vehicle maintenance and equipment storage building located in the eastern portion of the Site. This building is occupied daily by RES employees conducting fleet maintenance and equipment staging operations. A vapor intrusion assessment --- including sub-slab soil gas sampling and indoor air quality monitoring --- was not within the scope of this Phase II ESA but is recommended as an important follow-up investigation. If vapor intrusion is confirmed to be occurring at concentrations posing unacceptable risk to building occupants, occupational health measures and building mitigation systems (e.g., sub-slab depressurization) may be required. Elkhorn considers this a matter warranting prompt attention.
**[7. Remediation Cost Estimate]{.underline}**
Based on the findings of this Phase II ESA, Elkhorn has prepared an order-of-magnitude remediation cost estimate for addressing the identified soil and groundwater contamination at the Site. The estimate assumes continued commercial/industrial land use, consistent with current zoning and facility operations, and does not include costs for potential off-site remediation, if any is ultimately determined to be necessary.

**Important Caveats and Limitations**
This remediation cost estimate is subject to the following important caveats:
> \(a\) The estimate is based on subsurface conditions as observed during the April--May 2019 field investigation and does not account for potential changes in contaminant distribution, migration, or degradation that may have occurred since the investigation was completed. Contaminant conditions at the Site may have changed materially in the intervening period.
>
> \(b\) The estimate does not include costs for: (i) vapor intrusion assessment or mitigation of the eastern warehouse building; (ii) off-site groundwater remediation, if off-site plume migration is identified through additional investigation; (iii) potential third-party claims arising from environmental contamination; or (iv) natural resource damage claims.
>
> \(c\) The chlorinated solvent remediation in Area 2 carries significant cost uncertainty due to the potential for DNAPL migration to depths below the current investigation extent, which could substantially increase the volume of impacted subsurface media and the scope of remediation required.
>
> \(d\) Actual remediation costs may be higher than estimated if contaminant conditions have changed, if regulatory standards become more stringent, or if off-site migration is identified through additional investigation. Cost factors including labor rates, disposal fees, and equipment costs are presented in 2019 dollars and should be adjusted for inflation if applied at a future date.
>
> \(e\) Elkhorn recommends that this remediation cost estimate be updated periodically to reflect current site conditions and cost factors, and in particular that it be updated prior to any property transaction or financing event involving the Site.
**[8. Conclusions and Recommendations]{.underline}**
**8.1 Conclusions.** Based on the results of this Phase II ESA, Elkhorn presents the following conclusions:
> 1\. The Phase II ESA has confirmed the presence of significant soil and groundwater contamination at the Site resulting from historical industrial operations that pre-date RES\'s acquisition and occupancy of the Property in 2009. All contamination identified during this investigation is attributable to activities conducted by prior owners and operators of the facility.
>
> 2\. Petroleum hydrocarbon contamination, including TPH-diesel, TPH-gasoline, and BTEX compounds, is present in the western portion of the Site (former UST area) at concentrations exceeding applicable CDPHE commercial/industrial soil cleanup levels and Colorado Basic Standards for Groundwater.
>
> 3\. Chlorinated solvent contamination, including PCE, TCE, and the degradation product cis-1,2-DCE, is present in the eastern portion of the Site (former degreasing operations area) at concentrations exceeding applicable CDPHE soil cleanup levels and Colorado groundwater standards. The chlorinated solvent contamination poses the more complex and costly remediation challenge due to the chemical properties of the contaminants, their potential for continued vertical migration as DNAPLs, and the extended timeframes typically required for effective remediation of chlorinated solvent sites.
>
> 4\. All contamination identified at the Site is consistent with **gradual, long-term releases** from historical operations rather than acute, sudden, or accidental discharge events. This characterization is based on the spatial distribution of contaminants, the presence of reductive dechlorination byproducts, the diffuse plume geometry observed in both source areas, and the documented operational history of the Site spanning multiple decades of petroleum storage and chlorinated solvent usage.
>
> 5\. Elevated soil gas concentrations of PCE and TCE in the eastern portion of the Site indicate a potential vapor intrusion pathway affecting the 28,000-square-foot vehicle maintenance and equipment storage building, which is occupied daily by RES employees. This potential exposure pathway requires further evaluation through a dedicated vapor intrusion assessment.
>
> 6\. Groundwater contamination appears contained within the Site boundaries based on the existing monitoring well network; however, the current well coverage is limited and does not include off-site sentinel locations. Additional downgradient monitoring wells are required to confirm whether the plume has migrated beyond the Property boundary.
**8.2 Recommendations.** Elkhorn recommends the following actions:
> 1\. **Updated Site Characterization:** The monitoring well network should be expanded to include a minimum of two off-site downgradient wells positioned to intercept potential plume migration toward the northwest. At least two additional rounds of groundwater sampling should be conducted to establish seasonal variability and to evaluate plume stability. These activities are essential to define the full extent of groundwater contamination and to determine whether off-site impacts exist.
>
> 2\. **Vapor Intrusion Assessment:** Indoor air quality sampling and sub-slab soil gas sampling should be conducted in the eastern warehouse and vehicle maintenance building to evaluate whether chlorinated solvent vapors are intruding into the occupied structure at concentrations that may pose unacceptable health risk to building occupants.
>
> 3\. **Remediation Planning:** RES should initiate discussions with CDPHE regarding development of a voluntary cleanup plan under the Colorado Voluntary Cleanup and Redevelopment Program (\"VCUP\") to establish a clear regulatory framework and pathway for remediation of the identified contamination.
>
> 4\. **Periodic Re-assessment:** This Phase II ESA should be updated if significant time elapses before remediation commences, if there is a material change in Site use or operations, or in connection with any property transaction, financing event, or transfer of ownership, to ensure that the findings and cost estimates remain current and reliable.
>
> 5\. **Disclosure:** RES should ensure that any potential buyers, lenders, investors, or other parties with a financial interest in the Property are made aware of the environmental conditions documented herein, and that such parties are afforded the opportunity to review the full Phase II ESA report and to conduct independent investigation as they deem appropriate.
**8.3 Limitations.** This Executive Summary is a condensed presentation of findings from the full 180-page Phase II ESA report (Elkhorn Project No. EEC-2019-0347). Parties relying on this summary should review the complete report for full analytical data, boring logs, monitoring well construction details, laboratory certificates of analysis, and supporting figures and interpretive discussion.
The findings presented herein are based on a limited number of sampling points and analytical parameters, and may not fully characterize all subsurface conditions at the Site. Actual conditions between and beyond sampling points may differ from those presented in this report. Subsurface conditions are inherently variable, and no environmental investigation can eliminate all uncertainty regarding the nature and extent of contamination.
Environmental conditions at the Site may change over time due to natural processes (including contaminant migration, degradation, and seasonal water table fluctuations), human activities, or changes in applicable regulatory standards and screening criteria. The findings of this report are valid as of the date of the field investigation (April--May 2019) and **should not be relied upon as representative of conditions at any future date without updated investigation**. Elkhorn expressly recommends that any party intending to rely on this report in connection with a property transaction, financing, or similar event verify that the findings remain current by commissioning updated subsurface investigation.

**[II.A --- Calloway v. Harper Environmental Consulting, LLC]{.underline}**

**Parties:** Ridgeline Environmental Services, Inc. (Plaintiff) v. Harper Environmental Consulting, LLC (Defendant)
**Nature of Claims:** This matter arises from a breach of contract dispute with Harper Environmental Consulting, LLC (\"Harper\"), a former subcontractor that was engaged by RES to provide site characterization and sampling services on multiple environmental remediation projects during the 2021--2023 period. RES alleges that Harper failed to perform work in accordance with the contractual specifications set forth in the applicable task orders, delivered deficient and unreliable analytical reports that did not meet quality assurance and quality control standards, and caused significant project delays across several active remediation sites. These delays, in turn, resulted in liquidated damages charges being assessed against RES by its end clients under the prime contracts governing those remediation projects. RES further alleges that it was required to engage replacement subcontractors at premium rates to re-perform a substantial portion of the work originally contracted to Harper.
**Damages Sought:** RES is seeking approximately \$2.1 million in damages, comprising direct contract damages for the cost differential of re-performance, pass-through liquidated damages assessed by end clients attributable to Harper\'s delays, and ancillary costs associated with project remediation and schedule recovery.
**Current Status:** The matter is in the discovery phase. Depositions of Harper\'s project manager and RES\'s Vice President of Operations, Kurt Dillon, were completed during the third quarter of 2024. Written discovery is substantially complete, and expert reports are due in early 2025. A mediation session has been scheduled for February 2025 before a mutually agreed mediator. Harper has filed a counterclaim in the amount of \$340,000, alleging unpaid invoices for work performed under the subcontract agreements. RES disputes the counterclaim on the basis that the work to which the invoices relate was non-conforming and did not satisfy contractual acceptance criteria, thereby relieving RES of the obligation to pay the invoiced amounts.
**Management Assessment:** Management assesses the probability of a favorable outcome on RES\'s affirmative claims as Probable. Based on the strength of the documentary evidence and the deposition testimony obtained to date, management expects a net recovery in the range of \$800,000 to \$1.4 million after accounting for Harper\'s potential partial offset for any invoices that may ultimately be determined to have been for conforming work. Management characterizes this matter as a routine commercial dispute. It should be noted that the \$1.2 million litigation settlement referenced in the Company\'s FY2024 EBITDA adjustment schedule relates to a separate, previously resolved breach-of-contract matter --- specifically, the Clearwater Logistics dispute described in Section IV.A below --- and does not pertain to this case.

Plaintiff alleges that during the period from approximately March 2023 through January 2024, he was regularly exposed to volatile organic compounds (\"VOCs\") and heavy metals while performing field work at the site without adequate protective measures. Specifically, Plaintiff\'s complaint alleges that RES failed to provide adequate personal protective equipment, failed to conduct required air monitoring in accordance with applicable regulatory standards, and did not adhere to the site-specific health and safety plan developed for the Sheridan project. The complaint asserts claims for negligence, negligence per se based on alleged violations of Occupational Safety and Health Administration (\"OSHA\") regulations, and strict liability.
**Damages Sought:** Plaintiff seeks \$4.8 million in damages, comprising alleged medical expenses, lost wages, pain and suffering, and punitive damages.
**Current Status:** RES filed its Answer on October 7, 2024, denying the material allegations of the complaint and asserting affirmative defenses including comparative negligence and assumption of risk. RES has tendered the claim to Frontier Specialty Insurance Group under both its commercial general liability (\"CGL\") policy and its pollution liability policy. **Management Assessment:** Management assesses the probability of an adverse outcome as Reasonably Possible. Management\'s estimated range of loss, in the event of an adverse outcome, is \$500,000 to \$1,500,000. Management notes that (i) Plaintiff\'s medical records have not yet been fully reviewed and the nature and extent of any injury remain in dispute, (ii) causation is disputed, as Plaintiff has a documented history of occupational exposure at prior employers, and (iii) RES maintains that its safety protocols were followed in accordance with the site-specific health and safety plan and that all required PPE was provided and available to field personnel. **[III. Regulatory and Administrative Proceedings]{.underline}**
**[III.A --- Colorado Department of Public Health & Environment v. Ridgeline Environmental Services, Inc. (CDPHE Enforcement Action)]{.underline}**
**Forum:** Administrative Proceeding before the Colorado Department of Public Health & Environment (\"CDPHE\"), Hazardous Materials and Waste Management Division
**Docket Number:** CDPHE-HW-2024-0093
**Notice of Violation Issued:** July 18, 2024
**Facility:** Grand Junction headquarters and operations facility, located at 8750 Industrial Parkway, Grand Junction, CO 81505, operating under Colorado RCRA Part B Permit No. COD-098-2761
**Nature of Allegations:** CDPHE alleges that during the second quarter of 2024, RES stored hazardous waste in excess of the permitted volume and duration at its Grand Junction facility in violation of the terms and conditions of its RCRA Part B permit. Specifically, the Notice of Violation alleges that approximately 14,000 gallons of listed hazardous waste --- classified as F001/F002 spent solvents under 40 C.F.R. § 261.31 --- were stored in a temporary staging area on the facility premises that was not designated or authorized for storage under the facility\'s RCRA Part B permit. CDPHE further alleges that the waste remained in the unauthorized location beyond the 90-day generator accumulation period prescribed under 40 C.F.R. § 262.17, without a corresponding storage permit modification having been obtained from CDPHE.
**Key Dispute --- Violation Period:** The parties disagree on the duration of the alleged violation, which is a material determinant of the potential penalty amount.
> **Company Position:** RES self-reported the violation to CDPHE in June 2024, prior to CDPHE\'s compliance inspection of the facility. The Company asserts that the violation period was twelve (12) days, measured from the date on which the hazardous waste in the temporary staging area exceeded the 90-day accumulation limit to the date on which the waste was relocated to a permitted storage unit on-site. At the statutory maximum penalty of \$37,500 per day of violation under Section 3008(g) of the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (\"RCRA\"), the Company\'s calculated maximum exposure based on a 12-day violation period is **\$450,000** (12 days × \$37,500/day).
>
> **CDPHE Position:** CDPHE\'s Notice of Violation alleges that the violation period was thirty-one (31) days, based on CDPHE\'s determination --- derived from facility inspection records and waste manifesting data reviewed during the June 2024 compliance inspection --- that the unauthorized accumulation of waste in the staging area commenced on a date earlier than the Company has acknowledged. At the \$37,500 per-day statutory maximum, CDPHE\'s position implies a maximum penalty exposure of **\$1,162,500** (31 days × \$37,500/day).
The parties disagree on the commencement date of the violation. CDPHE\'s calculation includes a period during which the Company contends waste volumes had not yet exceeded permitted thresholds.
**Current Status:** The matter is in administrative negotiation. RES\'s environmental counsel submitted a detailed written response to the Notice of Violation on September 5, 2024, disputing the 31-day characterization and presenting operational logs, daily inspection records, and waste manifesting documentation in support of the Company\'s position that the violation period was limited to 12 days. CDPHE has not yet issued a formal penalty assessment or proposed consent order. A settlement conference is expected to be scheduled during the first quarter of 2025.
**Mitigating Factors Cited by Management:** Management has identified several factors that it believes support a favorable resolution:
> \(i\) RES self-reported the storage issue to CDPHE before the agency conducted its compliance inspection of the facility;
>
> \(ii\) the hazardous waste at issue was properly containerized in approved containers at all times during the alleged violation period and did not result in any release to the environment, the soil, or groundwater;
>
> \(iii\) RES has implemented corrective measures in response to the violation, including the addition of supplemental storage capacity and the adoption of revised internal inspection protocols and waste tracking procedures; and
>
> \(iv\) the Grand Junction facility has no prior RCRA violations in the approximately twelve years since the RCRA Part B permit was originally issued.
**Management Assessment:** Management assesses the probability of some penalty being assessed as Probable. Based on the Company\'s 12-day violation position, anticipated credit for self-reporting, and the mitigating factors described above, management\'s estimated settlement range is \$200,000 to \$450,000. Management considers the \$1,162,500 maximum penalty figure derived from CDPHE\'s 31-day position to be an opening negotiation position and does not view it as a likely outcome.
**Financial Impact:** No accrual has been recorded on the Company\'s balance sheet as of September 30, 2024 for CDPHE penalties related to this enforcement action. The Company\'s environmental remediation accrual of \$3.2 million, as reflected on the balance sheet, relates to facility remediation obligations --- primarily the Grand Junction soil contamination described in Section VI.A below and minor remediation obligations at other operating locations --- and does not include any provision for regulatory penalties. The CDPHE penalty exposure is not included in the Company\'s EBITDA adjustment schedule. To clarify, the \$1.2 million litigation settlement add-back referenced in the EBITDA adjustment schedule relates to a separate, previously resolved breach-of-contract dispute with Clearwater Logistics, Inc. (see Section IV.A below), and is not related to this CDPHE enforcement action.

**[VI. Potential Future Claims]{.underline}**
**[VI.A --- Grand Junction Facility Environmental Remediation Obligations]{.underline}**
The Company\'s Grand Junction facility at 8750 Industrial Parkway has documented soil contamination resulting from operations conducted by prior owners and operators of the site prior to RES\'s acquisition of the property in 2009. A Phase II Environmental Site Assessment was completed in June 2019 by Elkhorn Environmental Consultants, Inc. The Phase II ESA identified petroleum hydrocarbon and chlorinated solvent contamination in subsurface soils at the facility, with estimated remediation costs ranging from \$1.8 million to \$2.6 million (based on 2019 cost estimates). RES has accrued \$3.2 million on its balance sheet for environmental remediation obligations across all operating facilities, of which approximately \$2.2 million is attributable to the Grand Junction facility and the remainder relates to minor remediation obligations at other Company locations.
No updated Phase II Environmental Site Assessment has been commissioned since the 2019 assessment. Management is not aware of any material change in site conditions since the 2019 ESA was completed, although CDPHE has not required updated site characterization to date. Remediation work at the Grand Junction facility has been limited to monitoring activities.
**Management Assessment:** Remediation is expected to be required, but the timing and specific scope of remediation activities remain uncertain and are subject to CDPHE\'s regulatory direction. Management believes the current accrual of \$2.2 million (within the \$3.2 million total) is adequate to address the remediation obligations at Grand Junction based on the 2019 ESA estimate. Probability of remediation obligation: Probable. Estimated loss range: \$1.8 million to \$2.6 million (per the 2019 ESA).
**[VI.B --- Asbestos Abatement Long-Tail Exposure]{.underline}**
RES operated an asbestos abatement service line from approximately 2012 through September 30, 2023, when the service line was formally discontinued as part of a strategic decision to focus the Company\'s operations on its core environmental remediation and waste management services. During the period of operation, RES performed asbestos abatement work at approximately 145 commercial and industrial sites across Colorado, Utah, and Wyoming. RES maintained asbestos-specific liability insurance and complied with all applicable regulations under the National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants (\"NESHAP\") and OSHA asbestos standards during the period of operations.
As with any entity that has performed asbestos abatement activities, there exists the potential for long-tail personal injury claims from employees or third parties alleging asbestos exposure during the course of abatement work. No such claims have been asserted to date. The Company\'s current pollution liability policy, issued by Frontier Specialty Insurance Group, contains coverage for completed operations, with a retroactive date of January 1, 2015. This policy would provide coverage for claims arising from work performed from January 1, 2015 forward. Claims arising from work performed prior to January 1, 2015 --- that is, work conducted during the period from 2012 through 2014 --- may not be covered under the current policy, as those operations predate the retroactive date.
**Management Assessment:** Management assesses the probability of future asbestos-related personal injury claims as Remote. Management notes the relatively small scale of the asbestos abatement operation, the Company\'s consistent adherence to all applicable regulatory protocols, and the use of proper containment and abatement procedures throughout the service line\'s operation.
**Financial Impact:** No accrual has been recorded and no specific reserve has been established for potential future asbestos-related claims. The wind-down costs for the asbestos abatement service line totaled approximately \$1.8 million in FY2024, consisting primarily of employee severance payments, equipment decommissioning costs, and regulatory close-out expenses. These wind-down costs have been included in the Company\'s EBITDA adjustment schedule as a non-recurring add-back.

The Company has undertaken interim groundwater monitoring consistent with Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment guidance, but active remediation has not commenced.

**[Section 4: Detailed Lease Summaries --- Key Provisions]{.underline}**
**4.1 Salt Lake City Transfer Station --- Detailed Provisions**
**Lease Agreement.** Commercial Lease Agreement dated April 1, 2019 (the \"SLC Lease\"), by and between Wasatch Industrial Properties, LLC, a Utah limited liability company (\"Landlord\"), and Pinnacle Waste Solutions, LLC, a Utah limited liability company (\"Tenant\").
**Premises.** Approximately 22,000 square feet of warehouse and transfer station space situated on approximately 3.8 acres, including a concrete pad, four loading docks, and a fenced outdoor storage area. The facility is used for hazardous and non-hazardous waste transfer, storage, and processing operations.
**Base Rent and Escalation.** The initial base rent under the SLC Lease is \$28,500 per month, subject to an annual escalation of 2.5% on each anniversary of the lease commencement date. Based on the escalation schedule, the current effective rent for the lease year commencing April 1, 2024 is approximately \$31,475 per month. The lease is structured on a triple net (NNN) basis; the tenant is responsible for all property taxes, insurance premiums, and maintenance and repair costs.
**Permitted Use.** The permitted use under the SLC Lease includes hazardous and non-hazardous waste transfer, storage, and processing operations, subject to all applicable federal, state, and local laws and regulations.
**Assignment and Subletting (Section 14 of the SLC Lease).** Section 14 of the SLC Lease provides, in relevant part:
> \"Tenant shall not assign this Lease or any interest therein, or sublet the Premises or any part thereof, or permit the use of the Premises by any party other than Tenant, without the prior written consent of Landlord, which consent shall not be unreasonably withheld, conditioned, or delayed. Any change of control of Tenant (whether by merger, consolidation, sale of equity interests, or otherwise) shall be deemed an assignment requiring Landlord\'s consent under this Section.\"
**Status of Assignment.** Following the acquisition of Pinnacle Waste Solutions, LLC by RES on March 15, 2022, RES submitted a written request for consent to assignment to Wasatch Industrial Properties, LLC on April 12, 2022. As of the date of this Schedule, the Landlord has not provided written consent or acknowledgment of the assignment. RES has been in occupancy of the premises and paying rent continuously since March 15, 2022. All rent payments have been accepted by the Landlord without objection, and no notice of default has been received from the Landlord. Copies of the assignment request letter, follow-up correspondence dated July 8, 2022 and November 14, 2022, and records of rent payments are available in Data Room Folder 3.04.
**Proposed Transaction Implications.** The proposed acquisition of 100% of the outstanding common stock of RES by Sycamore Capital Partners, LP may constitute an additional change-of-control event under Section 14 of the SLC Lease, potentially requiring a separate consent from the Landlord. Transaction counsel should evaluate whether the SLC Lease requires fresh consent for the proposed transaction independent of the Pinnacle-to-RES assignment, and whether the absence of Landlord consent to the initial assignment creates a pre-existing default condition under the lease.
**Hazardous Waste Permit Cross-Reference.** The Utah Division of Waste Management Permit No. UTH-0441 for the Salt Lake City transfer station was originally issued to Pinnacle Waste Solutions, LLC and has not been formally transferred to RES. The Company is currently operating the facility under Pinnacle\'s permit. Refer to the Environmental Permit Schedule (Data Room Item 2.07) for complete details regarding permit transfer status.
**4.2 Ogden Transfer Station --- Detailed Provisions**
**Lease Agreement.** Commercial Lease Agreement dated July 1, 2020, by and between Northgate Commercial Realty, LLC (\"Landlord\") and Pinnacle Waste Solutions, LLC (\"Tenant\"). The lease was originally executed by Pinnacle and was subsequently assigned to Ridgeline Environmental Services, Inc. effective June 1, 2022, with the written consent of the Landlord obtained on May 15, 2022.
**Base Rent and Escalation.** The initial base rent is \$18,750 per month, subject to a 2% annual escalation. The lease is structured as a modified gross lease with the tenant responsible for utilities and interior maintenance.
**Assignment.** The Ogden lease contains an assignment provision substantially similar to that in the Salt Lake City lease, requiring prior written consent of the Landlord, which consent shall not be unreasonably withheld. RES requested and obtained landlord consent to the assignment from Pinnacle to RES in May 2022, and the assignment was completed without incident.
**Permit Cross-Reference.** Utah Division of Waste Management Permit No. UTH-0587 for the Ogden transfer station was originally issued to Pinnacle and was formally transferred to RES in June 2022. The assignment and permit transfer for the Ogden facility have been fully completed. No outstanding issues exist with respect to this lease.
**4.3 Casper Operations Facility --- Detailed Provisions**
**Lease Agreement.** Commercial Lease Agreement dated March 1, 2019, by and between Platte River Industrial Holdings, LLC (\"Landlord\") and Ridgeline Environmental Services, Inc. (\"Tenant\"). RES is the original tenant on this lease; no assignment was required in connection with the Pinnacle acquisition.
**Base Rent.** \$22,000 per month for the initial 10-year term. The single 5-year renewal option provides for rent at 3% annual escalation from the then-current rate.
**Assignment.** The lease contains a standard landlord consent requirement for assignment or subletting. No change-of-control provision is specifically defined, though the general assignment clause may apply to a change-of-control transaction depending on its structure.
**Permit Cross-Reference.** The facility operates under Wyoming Permit No. WY-HW-2019-033. A renewal application was filed on October 15, 2024; the current permit expired November 30, 2024. The facility is operating under timely renewal provisions in accordance with Wyoming Department of Environmental Quality regulations. No outstanding issues have been identified.
**4.4 Other Leased Facilities --- Summary Notes**
**Billings Operations Facility.** The Billings lease is current through January 14, 2027, with one 3-year renewal option available. The facility operates under Montana Permit No. MT-HW-2022-011, which is current through March 2027. No outstanding lease or permit issues have been identified at this location.
**Boise Emergency Response Depot.** The Boise facility serves as an emergency response staging area only. Idaho operations are limited to emergency response activities, and no hazardous waste storage or treatment permit is required for operations at this location. **Denver Administrative Office.** The Denver lease covers an administrative and business development office and does not involve any environmental permitting. The lease is current through May 31, 2026, with one 2-year renewal option. The facility houses the Company\'s Vice President of Business Development, Sandra Oakes, and four support staff members.
**Pueblo Storage Yard.** The Pueblo lease expires on April 30, 2025, which coincides with the target closing date for the proposed transaction. The facility is used for equipment and vehicle storage, and the lease automatically converts to month-to-month tenancy following expiration. Renewal terms are currently under negotiation with the landlord, Arkansas Valley Land Co., LLC. If the lease is not renewed on acceptable terms, equipment and vehicles housed at the Pueblo yard will need to be relocated to another Company facility. No environmental permits are associated with this location.
**Rock Springs Field Office.** The Rock Springs lease is a standard commercial lease current through October 31, 2026. No renewal options are available under the existing lease terms. No material issues have been identified.
**Missoula Staging Area.** The Missoula lease is current through March 31, 2026, with one 2-year renewal option. The facility is a small staging and storage location supporting western Montana project operations. The lease contains no restriction on assignment. No material issues have been identified.
**Cheyenne Equipment Yard.** The Cheyenne lease is current through July 31, 2027, with one 3-year renewal option. The facility is used for equipment storage and light maintenance. The lease requires landlord consent for assignment. No material issues have been identified.

           "QoE 'Revenue by Customer' tab (e.g., Western Slope Energy Partners, Rio Tinto Kennecott, Suncor, Freeport-McMoRan, Marathon, "
           "Newmont, Chevron). Yet both total $127.3M and both show top-10 concentration of exactly 67.0%. The CIM's Customers C/D/E "

           "(the true top-10 share is $89.2M, or 70.1%). 'All other' revenue is $13.8M (~85 customers), $19.1M (~120 accounts) or "
